title: Guedes v. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives
lead: Challenges to a new bump-stock rule brought together firearm classification, rulemaking procedure, and the authority of Acting Attorney General Matthew Whitaker. The district court rejected three requests for preliminary injunctions, leaving the broader lawsuits and several merits questions unresolved.

actors.name: Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF)
actors.role: Federal agency that adopted the December 2018 bump-stock rule.

actors.name: Damien Guedes and associated organizations
actors.role: Challengers principally asserting statutory and administrative defects.

actors.name: Firearms Policy Coalition
actors.role: Organization separately challenging Whitaker’s statutory and constitutional authority.

actors.name: David Codrea
actors.role: Plaintiff in a related action also asserting a taking.

actors.name: Matthew Whitaker
actors.role: Acting Attorney General who served after Jeff Sessions’s resignation.

actors.name: William Barr
actors.role: Successor Attorney General substituted as defendant.

actors.name: Judge Dabney Friedrich
actors.role: District judge deciding the three preliminary-injunction motions.

proceedings: Related and partly consolidated district-court actions produced three motions for preliminary injunctions. Judge Friedrich denied all three on February 25, 2019, finding no sufficient likelihood of success; this was not a final dismissal or appellate ruling.
limits: The statutory analysis uses Chevron as applied in February 2019 and does not certify later bump-stock law or current deference doctrine. The court reserved whether a compensable taking occurred. Whitaker’s temporary service, rather than a conclusion that he was already an officer as chief of staff, supported the appointment analysis.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: ATF revisits how bump stocks operate under the machine-gun definition
sections.cue: What had the agency previously distinguished?
paragraphs: After the October 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) reconsidered bump stocks. A standard version replaced a semiautomatic rifle’s stock and allowed recoil to move the weapon against a maintained trigger finger. ATF had previously excluded those devices because it considered their firing insufficiently automatic. In 2006 it had classified the spring-equipped Akins Accelerator as a machine gun. The parties agreed on basic mechanics; legal classification was disputed.

The National Firearms Act defined machinegun by automatic firing of more than one shot, without manual reloading, through a single trigger function, and included certain conversion parts and combinations. The Firearm Owners Protection Act incorporated that definition and generally prohibited possession or transfer of newly manufactured machine guns.

sections.title: A temporary Attorney General serves as the rule reaches completion
sections.cue: How did the appointment and the new regulation converge?
paragraphs: Attorney General Jeff Sessions resigned in November 2018. The President selected Sessions’s chief of staff, Matthew Whitaker, to exercise the Attorney General’s duties under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA). The parties did not dispute that Whitaker met §3345(a)(3)’s service and senior-pay eligibility requirements: ninety of the preceding 365 days as an agency officer or employee at the specified level.

Under the Attorney General’s rulemaking authority, ATF published its final rule on December 26, 2018. It construed a single trigger function as one pull or analogous motion, and automatic firing as a self-acting or self-regulating mechanism permitting multiple rounds through that function. It expressly classified bump-stock-type devices as machine guns. Owners would have to destroy or abandon them when the rule took effect March 26, 2019.

sections.title: Three sets of challengers seek immediate relief
sections.cue: Which claims and cases were before Friedrich?
paragraphs: Damien Guedes and associated organizations initially sued together on December 18, 2018. The Firearms Policy Coalition dismissed its claims from that action and filed separately, emphasizing Whitaker’s authority. Its suit was later consolidated with Guedes. David Codrea’s separate suit was transferred as related but, at the parties’ request, remained unconsolidated. Guedes’s amended complaint omitted the appointment challenge, which other plaintiffs still presented.

The challengers alleged unlawful statutory interpretation and defects in explanation, disclosure, and responses to comments under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Guedes also raised statutory hearing and ninety-day notice requirements. Codrea asserted a taking, and the Coalition developed the vacancies-statute and Appointments Clause objections.

Government-shutdown stays, their subsequent lifting, and hearings preceded the February 25 decision. By then William Barr had replaced Whitaker after approximately one hundred days of acting service and was automatically substituted under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 25(d). Judge Dabney Friedrich resolved all three preliminary-injunction motions.

sections.title: The judge finds the agency’s statutory construction permissible under the then-governing framework
sections.cue: Why did the mechanical trigger reset not decide the case?
paragraphs: Preliminary relief required a clear showing of likely success, likely irreparable harm, favorable equities, and consistency with the public interest. Failure on likelihood of success made the other factors unnecessary. Under the then-governing Chevron framework, clear statutory instructions controlled, while a permissible interpretation of ambiguity received deference.

Contemporary dictionaries did not resolve whether a single trigger function meant each mechanical reset or the shooter’s initiating pull. Both readings were reasonable. Decisions including Staples and Akins had described machine guns using a single-pull concept, supporting ATF’s approach. Dictionaries described automatic mechanisms as self-acting but did not specify how much human input was permissible; even an automatic sewing machine required input.

ATF could therefore treat maintained pressure and recoil-directed firing as a single pull followed by automatic operation. Repeated contact between trigger and finger did not require repeated conscious pulls. Ordinary semiautomatic rifles without the device still required a separate pull for each cartridge. Automatic operation was the closer issue because the shooter maintained pressure, but the device managed recoil distance and linear movement otherwise controlled manually. Friedrich found ATF’s interpretation reasonable, not the only possible textual reading.

sections.title: ATF’s changed explanation and responses survive the preliminary challenge
sections.cue: Why did the judge reject disclosure and comment objections?
paragraphs: A policy change required acknowledgment and good reasons, not an extra substantive burden solely because the policy differed. ATF acknowledged its prior classifications, discussed the Akins history, and explained why the new legal analysis better read the terms. Earlier standard-bump-stock determinations contained little developed legal reasoning.

Those old legal opinions were not critical factual support that had to be disclosed for rebuttal: the device’s operation was undisputed, and the opinions contradicted the new position. The Las Vegas shooting prompted reconsideration, but crime statistics were not the rule’s evidentiary premise.

Objections involving comparative firing speeds, a former official’s views, and a demonstration video did not show inadequate explanation. Classification concerned device function, not whether an unaided shooter could fire faster. ATF had to answer significant relevant objections, not discuss every submission individually. It addressed operational arguments, distinguished belt loops and rubber bands as manual methods without a recoil-capturing device while leaving their formal classification unresolved, and explained that binary triggers used separate pull and release functions. Those responses satisfied the APA at this stage.

sections.title: Written participation suffices, and the taking claim does not support this injunction
paragraphs: Section 926(b)’s opportunity-for-hearing language did not require an oral hearing. Following Florida East Coast Railway’s approach to hearing language and Fourth Circuit interpretation of this provision, Friedrich found written comments sufficient without an on-the-record requirement.

Technical difficulties affected the first five days of the scheduled ninety-day comment period. But the proper Regulations.gov page was accessible, some comments arrived, mail and facsimile remained available, and online submissions continued for the other eighty-five days. Guedes showed no prejudice; failure to extend was harmless.

Codrea’s takings theory did not justify an injunction regardless of its merits. The Takings Clause generally secured compensation rather than forbidding an authorized taking before payment. No inadequacy of Tucker Act or Little Tucker Act compensation, or applicable exception, had been shown. Friedrich reserved whether the rule effected a compensable taking.

sections.title: The succession statute provides an alternative rather than an exclusive sequence
sections.cue: Why could the President use the FVRA?
paragraphs: The Coalition argued that 28 U.S.C. §508 required exhaustion of the Deputy Attorney General, Associate Attorney General, and further designated successors before resort to the FVRA. Friedrich read §3347 differently: another applicable succession statute made the FVRA nonexclusive, not unavailable. Hooks and English supported coexistence of statutory routes.

Congress removed the former Attorney General exception when adopting the FVRA, and §508 expressly designated the Deputy as first assistant for §3345 purposes. Mandatory exhaustion would deprive that cross-reference of sensible effect. Section 508 said the Deputy may serve; its shall provision for the Associate governed when the President did not choose the FVRA route and the Deputy was unavailable.

Specific-over-general reasoning did not displace either provision because their eligibility and duration requirements differed. Earlier-bill legislative history supported an alternative mechanism, while vague references to exceptions did not overcome the enacted structure. Friedrich nevertheless rejected the Government’s claim that a few recent designations proved congressional acquiescence. Constitutional avoidance supplied no contrary interpretation because the text resolved the question and the appointment did not raise the asserted serious doubt.

sections.title: Temporary service does not turn every acting head into a permanent principal officer
sections.cue: How did the Appointments Clause analysis address supervision?
paragraphs: The Coalition contended that an unconfirmed acting head could serve only as a first assistant whose existing duties included substitution. Friedrich instead applied Eaton, which held that performing a superior’s duties for a limited time under special temporary conditions did not transform a subordinate into a permanent principal officer. Eaton’s missionary had been appointed shortly before a consul’s departure, weakening the proposed continuous-supervision explanation. Morrison and Edmond had preserved its temporary-service reasoning.

Early statutes permitted broad presidential choices for temporary vacancies; later statutes narrowed candidates and duration. Practice included chief clerks, other department heads, and some people outside government. Friedrich viewed temporary service, rather than prior first-assistant status, as the justification.

After a superior’s death or resignation, an assistant was not supervised during the very period needing explanation. Anticipated ratification could equally support another acting official. Earlier Senate confirmation to an unrelated office did not answer the question unless the duties were germane. Congress could tighten the rules, and courts could reject effectively permanent appointments disguised as temporary, but plaintiffs did not claim Whitaker’s hundred days were such a pretext.

sections.title: Alternative appointment arguments do not change the result
sections.cue: What exactly did the court deny?
paragraphs: Friedrich assumed without deciding that Whitaker previously was an employee and needed an appointment. Presidential designation under the FVRA constituted an appointment; Congress did not need a particular word. Weiss’s military-assignment analysis concerned whether a second appointment was necessary, not whether Congress’s grant failed for lack of terminology.

Conversely, if the plaintiffs’ continuing-position theory meant the temporary duties could not make Whitaker an officer at all, it would remove the constitutional need for appointment rather than invalidate his service. The court thus rejected the alternative challenges without simply assuming that his chief-of-staff post already made him an inferior officer.

On February 25, 2019, Friedrich denied all three preliminary-injunction motions. She did not finally dismiss the complaints, decide the takings merits, or issue an appellate affirmance. There was no separate opinion. Later appeals and changes in bump-stock or administrative-law doctrine were separate proceedings and developments.
